title: Wonder marks the way
hookLine: Lalla of Kashmir searches far for Shiva and finds him at home, and a Shiva Sutra says wonder marks the way
carry: wonder marks the way to shiva
tomorrow: if the self is a dancer, who's watching?

cards: A woman walks out of her house in Kashmir, about seven hundred years ago, and doesn't go back. Tradition remembers her as Lalla, or Lal Ded, Grandmother Lal.
The stories say her married life was hard, and that she left to follow a teacher of Shiva and wander as a yogini, singing. Her short Kashmiri sayings, called vakhs, are still on people's lips there.
And one of them tells how all her searching ended.

teach.b: In that saying, as it's usually rendered, Lalla says she went out searching far and wide, and when at last she found the one she was looking for, he was in her own house.
Another tells that her teacher gave her just one instruction: turn from what's outside to what's within. She took it so to heart that she began to dance.

That's the feeling the Shiva Sutras name in one thread: vismayo yogabhumikah. Vismaya is wonder, astonishment, the wide-eyed surprise of seeing something as if for the first time. Yogabhumikah: the stages of yoga.
Together: on this path, wonder is how you can tell you're on the way. Not pride. Not I've earned this.
Something more like: oh. This was here the whole time? Go back to the first two threads.

Consciousness is the self, Shiva's own. Knowing binds: the small sense of I am only this. When the small picture slips, commentators describe the yogi's response as delight, astonishment, because nothing new arrived.
What was always home is finally seen.
Wonder is what recognition feels like from the inside.

teach.h: WONDER MARKS THE STAGES OF YOGA.
teach.b: Lalla's sayings belong to more than one family.
Kashmiri Hindus call her Lal Ded and Lalleshwari; many Kashmiri Muslims love her too, and some call her Lalla Arifa, the one who knows.
Their prayers are honestly different, and the shared thing is plain: God near enough to be found at home. So the week ends on one small word: oh.

how: Students of Kashmir Shaivism read the Shiva Sutras with a teacher and a commentary, and Lal Ded's Kashmiri sayings are still recited and sung in Kashmir and by Kashmiri families abroad.

games.q: you're Lalla. you searched far and wide for Shiva, and you find him in your own house. by the Shiva Sutras, what fits?
o: wonder: oh, he was here all along.
disappointment that the search was for nothing.
games.why: vismayo yogabhumikah: wonder marks the stages of yoga. finding what was always home feels like oh.

practice: Choose something right in front of you, your hand, a cup, the light on a wall, and look at it as if for the first time: its color, its edges, the fact that it's here at all; when the mind says it's just a cup, look again.
Then turn the same wonder inward, on the plain fact that you're aware of anything, the thing Lalla found at home. If you pray, let that wonder be your prayer; if you don't, just stay with the oh.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir Shaivism opening. A thread from the Shiva Sutras: vismayo yogabhumikah, wonder marks the stages of yoga, the oh of finding Shiva at home.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a Shiva Sutra, wonder (vismaya) marks the stages (bhumika) of yoga.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder marks the way to Shiva. Lalla searched far, and found him at home. Seven days, ending on oh.
